## CompositeRiskValidator

Qualified name: <code>Meridian.Risk.CompositeRiskValidator</code>. Kind: `class`.

Source: [src/Meridian.Risk/CompositeRiskValidator.cs:28](../../../../src/Meridian.Risk/CompositeRiskValidator.cs#L28).

Composite risk validator that runs multiple risk rules in sequence, mapping each rule&#x27;s severity to a real outcome: RiskRuleSeverity.Info / RiskRuleSeverity.Warning — the breach becomes a warning flag on the result and evaluation continues. RiskRuleSeverity.Error — the order is rejected. RiskRuleSeverity.Escalate (or a rule returning RiskValidationResult.Escalated) — the order is parked in the governed approval queue instead of routed; a valid one-shot approval token on the order releases it past the escalation. RiskRuleSeverity.Critical — the order is rejected and the execution circuit breaker trips, halting all further routing until an operator closes it; when an ICircuitBreakerTripHandler is composed, the trip is followed by the kill-switch cancel-all sweep of the open book, mirroring the operator endpoint&#x27;s activation. Rules evaluate by priority; warning flags accumulate across rules and are carried on the final result whether approved or not.

## ICircuitBreakerTripHandler

Qualified name: <code>Meridian.Risk.ICircuitBreakerTripHandler</code>. Kind: `interface`.

Source: [src/Meridian.Risk/ICircuitBreakerTripHandler.cs:17](../../../../src/Meridian.Risk/ICircuitBreakerTripHandler.cs#L17).

Follow-up action invoked after CompositeRiskValidator trips the execution circuit breaker on a critical breach. The production registration sweeps the open order book (IOrderManager.CancelAllAsync), coupling the automated halt to the same cancel-all the operator kill-switch endpoint performs — a breaker that merely blocks new submissions leaves resting orders filling while routing is &quot;halted&quot;. The handler runs strictly after the trip: it must never gate, delay, or revert the halt. Implementations should report their own outcome (structured logs, audit trail) rather than throw; the validator suppresses any escaping exception so a failed sweep cannot leak back into the pre-trade risk path. Hosts without an order manager simply leave this unregistered and keep trip-only behavior.

BarClose and reaches for the touch only when neither exists. Anything that checks the quote earlier disagrees with it whenever the two differ, and it does so in both directions: with a 100/120 quote and the last trade at 100, a buy stop at 105 is resting but reads 4.5% crossed against the 110 midpoint and worse against the 120 ask — a false rejection; while a buy stop above the ask but below the last trade looks correctly placed as the matcher fires it — a false approval, and an unbounded market order. The bar close earns its place for the same reason: on a bar-driven session there is no print, and skipping to the quote reproduces the false approval in different clothing — no print, a 130 close, a 100 ask, and a buy stop at 125 reads as resting while the matcher triggers it. All three legs, in this order, or the control and the engine disagree somewhere. This deliberately differs from TryGetTouchPrice, which is what a limit is measured against — a limit trades at the touch, so for a limit the touch is not a fallback but the answer. |

## IReservingRiskRule

Qualified name: <code>Meridian.Risk.IReservingRiskRule</code>. Kind: `interface`.

Source: [src/Meridian.Risk/IRiskRule.cs:56](../../../../src/Meridian.Risk/IRiskRule.cs#L56).

Implemented by rules that consume finite capacity across orders (rate windows, burst counters). The reservation is taken during evaluation, under whatever lock the rule already holds, so the check and the consumption stay atomic. Splitting them across two calls would let concurrent submissions each observe room below the cap and all commit, overshooting it.

```csharp
public interface IReservingRiskRule : IRiskRule
```

Declared public members:

| Declaration | Source | Summary |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <code>Task&lt;RiskRuleReservationResult&gt; EvaluateAndReserveAsync(OrderRequest request, CancellationToken ct = default);</code> | [src/Meridian.Risk/IRiskRule.cs:73](../../../../src/Meridian.Risk/IRiskRule.cs#L73) | Atomically evaluates and, when the rule is satisfied, reserves the capacity this order would consume. The reservation is non-null whenever capacity was taken, and must be settled by the caller on every path. An implementation that has taken capacity must not let an exception escape before returning it. The handle reaches the validator only through the returned result, so a task that faults or cancels after reserving strands the capacity where nothing can release it — not the validator, which never saw it, and not the abandonment cleanup, which needs a completed task to read the handle from. The leak is permanent, and repeated failures would eventually block every order. Observe the token before reserving, not after; reserve and return in one uninterruptible step, as OrderRateThrottle does under its lock; or release the capacity in a catch before rethrowing. |

## BracketChildLimbRule

Qualified name: <code>Meridian.Risk.Rules.BracketChildLimbRule</code>. Kind: `class`.

Source: [src/Meridian.Risk/Rules/BracketChildLimbRule.cs:52](../../../../src/Meridian.Risk/Rules/BracketChildLimbRule.cs#L52).

Price-sanity gate for bracket/OCO child limbs — the take-profit and stop-loss prices an order carries in metadata and the gateway routes as broker-side child legs the moment the parent is accepted. Without this rule those prices reach the broker having passed no risk decision at all: FatFingerRule and PriceCollarRule measure only the parent&#x27;s own typed prices. Each limb is measured with exactly the machinery the parent&#x27;s prices are measured with — OrderPriceLimbs resolves what each price is meaningful against, the shared F# band evaluates it, and the operator&#x27;s one fat-finger deviation tolerance is the band. The limbs are the exit legs of the entry, so each is evaluated as the child order it becomes: the opposite side of the parent, the take-profit as a limit against the touch, the stop-loss trigger against the matcher&#x27;s trigger reference with the mirrored orientation, and a stop-loss limit against its own trigger. A limb that is individually plausible can still be structurally absurd as a pair — a long exit whose take-profit sits at or below its stop-loss can never bracket the market — so the pair&#x27;s ordering is checked too, first and without needing market data, for the same reason the fat-finger quantity limb is settled before the price limbs: a definitive breach must not be downgraded to a pricing-data gap. Deliberate boundary: price sanity only — the child limbs reserve no notional or gross-exposure capacity. They are contingent exit legs that close the position the parent opens, and under one-cancels-other semantics at most one of them ever executes, so reserving both against the exposure ceilings would double-count risk the parent&#x27;s own reservation already carries. Reservation-aware OCO arithmetic — reserve the worse limb, release on the sibling&#x27;s cancel — remains future work for the pre-trade gate; until it exists this rule keeps a mistyped exit price out of the market without pretending to be an exposure control. Fail-closed to match the parent bands: with the deviation band configured, a bracket whose symbol has no reference price is refused as unmeasurable rather than approved — a band an unpriceable limb sails past is not a band — and the refusal is reported as unmeasurable so a pricing gap cannot trip the circuit breaker. A null or non-positive band (the first-run defaults model) disarms the rule entirely, so the limbs pass exactly as the parent&#x27;s own prices would. Orders carrying no bracket metadata are untouched, and a multi-leg package is excluded for the same reason OrderPriceLimbs.AppliesTo excludes it: its prices belong to the combination, not the top-level symbol. A limb price the gateway would route but that is not positive is skipped exactly as the parent&#x27;s own non-positive prices are — the broker refuses that shape loudly on its own.

## FatFingerRule

Qualified name: <code>Meridian.Risk.Rules.FatFingerRule</code>. Kind: `class`.

Source: [src/Meridian.Risk/Rules/FatFingerRule.cs:96](../../../../src/Meridian.Risk/Rules/FatFingerRule.cs#L96).

Blocks the classic order-entry mistakes: a quantity far larger than the desk ever intends to send in one order, a price typed far through the market, and a stop whose trigger is on the wrong side of it. The price limb is deliberately directional. A resting buy far below the market and a resting sell far above it are ordinary working orders, so only the aggressive side is measured — paying above the reference on a buy, or selling below it on a sell. A symmetric band would reject the entire resting book. Every price this rule measures is measured against the reference that price is actually meaningful to, and each order type contributes only the prices it genuinely puts at risk of a typo: OrderType.Limit — its OrderRequest.LimitPrice is measured against the current touch. This is the only type whose limit is meaningful against the current continuous market, which is the only market this rule can see. OrderType.StopMarket — its OrderRequest.StopPrice is measured against IPortfolioExposureProvider.TryGetTriggerReferencePrice, not the touch, and with the mirrored orientation described below. That seam resolves the last trade, then the bar close, then the crossing side — the matcher&#x27;s precedence, which differs from the touch on any wide book. A stop is not measured for being far from the market — that is what a stop is — but for being on the wrong side of it, which is not a stop at all. OrderType.StopLimit — both. Its trigger is measured like a stop-market trigger, and its limit is measured against its own trigger rather than the market, because that is what the limit is priced off: a sell stop at $90 with an $89 limit is an ordinary protective order, 1.1% from its trigger, though it is 11% from a $100 market. OrderType.Market is excluded even when it carries a OrderRequest.LimitPrice. The paper gateway lets a caller supply one as its simulated market observation, so on a market order that value is not an operator&#x27;s typed limit and must not be compared against the live book. OrderType.LimitOnOpen and OrderType.LimitOnClose carry a broker-enforced limit, but this rule has no indicative-auction or prior-close reference. They therefore fail closed as unmeasurable while the deviation band is configured rather than comparing an auction price with the unrelated continuous touch or routing it unchecked. OrderType.TrailingStop is excluded: its trigger is derived by the broker from OrderRequest.TrailPrice or OrderRequest.TrailPercent and moves with the market, so comparing a snapshot of it against the current touch measures nothing that stays true. A multi-leg order is excluded entirely: its limit is the net debit or credit for the package, which is not comparable to a quote for the top-level symbol. A $1 credit spread on a $200 underlying would otherwise look 99.5% through the market. A stop trigger&#x27;s aggressive direction is the exact mirror of a limit&#x27;s, and conflating the two is what makes a wrong-side stop invisible. Meridian.Execution.PaperMatching.PaperOrderMatchingPolicy fires a buy stop once the market reaches or passes above it and a sell stop once the market reaches or falls below it, so a correctly placed buy stop sits above the market. A buy stop typed beneath the market — $1 against a $100 book — is already crossed on arrival, and a stop-market order that triggers on acceptance routes as an unbounded market order with no price protection at all. That is the single most expensive shape a mistyped order can take here, so the trigger is settled before the limit. The quantity limb is likewise skipped when OrderRequest.Quantity is not a unit count. Alpaca-style broker-notional orders carry dollars in that field, while fixed-income orders carry face value in denominations from 1,000 through 1,000,000. Comparing either with a share/contract ceiling would reject ordinary orders, while raising that ceiling enough for face value would disable it for equities. Their economic size remains gated by OrderNotionalRule. Every order excluded from the price limb still passes through the applicable quantity limb, and every order&#x27;s economic size is still gated by OrderNotionalRule. With the deviation band configured, a priced order whose symbol has no reference price is REJECTED as unmeasurable rather than approved: a band an unpriceable order sails past is not a band. The rejection is reported as unmeasurable so a pricing gap does not trip the circuit breaker, matching OrderNotionalRule. null thresholds disable the corresponding limb, and an entirely unconfigured rule approves without measuring.

## OrderPriceLimbs

Qualified name: <code>Meridian.Risk.Rules.OrderPriceLimbs</code>. Kind: `class`.

Source: [src/Meridian.Risk/Rules/OrderPriceLimbs.cs:59](../../../../src/Meridian.Risk/Rules/OrderPriceLimbs.cs#L59).

Resolves the prices a pre-trade price control may measure, and the reference each is meaningful against — independently of any band. This exists so the fat-finger band and the price collar cannot disagree about what they are measuring while disagreeing only about how far is too far. The two rules differ by threshold and by severity, and by nothing else: which order shapes carry a measurable price, which reference each price is meaningful against, and which direction counts as aggressive are properties of the order, not of the band. Duplicating them would let one rule protect an order shape the other refuses, which is worse than either behaviour chosen deliberately.

Throttles order submission rate to prevent runaway algorithms. Capacity is consumed by reservation during evaluation rather than by enqueueing on the pass path. That keeps the purge → count → reserve sequence atomic under one lock, exactly as the original check-and-enqueue was, while letting the caller release the slot if the order is ultimately blocked by another rule or fails before reaching the venue. Counting an order that never routed would throttle later orders for no reason.

## PriceCollarRule

Qualified name: <code>Meridian.Risk.Rules.PriceCollarRule</code>. Kind: `class`.

Source: [src/Meridian.Risk/Rules/PriceCollarRule.cs:44](../../../../src/Meridian.Risk/Rules/PriceCollarRule.cs#L44).

Parks an order priced further through the market than the desk transacts without sign-off, so a human decides rather than the order routing on its own. This is the escalate-severity counterpart to FatFingerRule, and the distinction between them is the point. A fat finger is a mistake: nobody meant to send it, so offering an operator a release would be offering to confirm a typo, and the rule rejects at RiskRuleSeverity.Error. A collar breach is a decision: the price is aggressive but may be exactly what the desk intends in a fast market, so it is parked at RiskRuleSeverity.Escalate for someone to approve or refuse. Rejecting these would stop legitimate trading; approving them silently would remove the judgement the band exists to demand. The collar therefore sits inside the fat-finger band: it should be the tighter of the two, so ordinary aggressive orders escalate while genuinely mistyped ones are refused outright. The two bands are configured independently and this rule does not police that ordering — a collar set wider than the fat-finger band simply never fires, because the harder rule refuses first at FatFingerRule.Priority, which runs ahead of this one. Everything about what is measured comes from OrderPriceLimbs, shared with the fat-finger band, and the deviation itself is computed by the same F# policy the harder rule calls. The two controls differ by threshold and severity and by nothing else: a collar that disagreed with the fat-finger band about which order shapes carry a measurable price, or about which reference a price is meaningful against, would protect a shape the other refuses.

## SymbolConcentrationRule

Qualified name: <code>Meridian.Risk.Rules.SymbolConcentrationRule</code>. Kind: `class`.

Source: [src/Meridian.Risk/Rules/SymbolConcentrationRule.cs:16](../../../../src/Meridian.Risk/Rules/SymbolConcentrationRule.cs#L16).

Rejects orders that would concentrate a single symbol beyond the configured percentage of portfolio value. Inside the observe band (at or above ObserveBandFraction of the cap) the order still routes but carries a warning flag so the breach surfaces on the risk dashboard before it becomes blocking. A null cap means the rule is not configured and approves.

public sealed class SymbolConcentrationRule : IRiskRule
